155.title: The blessing before study
155.hook: before learning, a blessing to be busy with words of Torah
155.tomorrow: Camp 3 close: your week has a shape
155.howItsDone: Traditional Jews say the blessings over Torah study each morning as part of the morning prayers, and many say them again before a class or a study session.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hamaor shebah: the light inside the learning, for believers and questioners alike. Your line was the light inside it. Day one hundred fifty-five.

Before a meal, many Jews say a blessing: bread gets one, fruit gets one, even water gets one. You've met those. But there's a blessing for something you can't eat. Before opening a book of Torah, before the day's first lesson, traditional Jews stop and bless God, the way they would over bread. As if words were food. And the Talmud tells a startling story about what happens when this blessing is skipped.
screen: `BREAD GETS A BLESSING.` → `SO DOES LEARNING.` → `AS IF WORDS WERE FOOD.`

segments.voice: The blessing opens like the ones over bread and fruit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam. Blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe. Then: asher kid'shanu b'mitzvotav, who made us holy with his commandments, v'tzivanu la'asok b'divrei Torah, and commanded us to be busy with the words of Torah. That verb is the surprise. La'asok. Not to read. Not to know. To be busy with, engaged in, occupied by. The blessing doesn't ask you to finish Torah, or master it. It asks you to be in the middle of it, working on it, the way someone runs a shop. Many prayer books follow it with a line asking that the words be sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children. In traditional practice, these blessings are said once in the morning, and they cover the whole day's learning. Now the startling story. The Talmud asks why the land was lost in ancient times. It quotes the prophet Jeremiah asking the same thing, and answers in the name of the teacher Rav: because they did not bless the Torah first. They studied. They knew it. But they didn't stop first and treat it as a gift. One medieval commentator, the Ran, reads it this way: they studied, but didn't hold the Torah dear enough to bless it first. In that reading, the blessing is a doorway. It marks the words as a gift before the study, and the argument, begins.
screen: `BLESSED ARE YOU, LORD OUR GOD.` · `LA'ASOK: TO BE BUSY WITH.` · `SWEET IN OUR MOUTHS.` · `THEY DID NOT BLESS THE TORAH FIRST.` · then, large: `BLESS THE WORDS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Pick up anything you'll read today, a book, a letter, even a long message, or just picture it, and stop before the first word. If you pray, you can say the blessing's opening words, Baruch atah Adonai, or the whole line; if you don't, take one breath and remember that words are a gift someone gave you. Then read one sentence slowly.
La'asok. To be busy with: the surprising verb in the blessing said before study, which asks only that you be busy with Torah's words.
Your line: bless the words first. The study begins on the far side of that doorway. Until tomorrow.

156.title: Camp 3 close: your week has a shape
156.hook: Shabbat, blessings, holidays, study: a life with rhythm
156.howItsDone: Jews shape the week around Shabbat, the day around prayer and blessings, and the year around the festivals; how many of these practices a person keeps varies widely across communities and families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, la'asok: be busy with the words of Torah. Your line was bless the words first. Today is the last day of this camp, a look back at all of it.

For a lot of people, a week goes like this. Monday blurs into Thursday. The weekend fills up with errands. Holidays sneak up and pass. It's a line with no shape, just more. This camp's sixty days began with a promise: I can do this. Not believe this. Do this. A candle, a cup, a blessing, a breath. Judaism answers the shapeless week with rhythm. Every day has its words, every week has its peak, every year has its seasons. Today, before a new camp begins, a walk back through what you've practiced, and a choice of what to keep.
screen: `I CAN DO THIS.` → `A WEEK WITH NO SHAPE.` → `A LIFE WITH RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: It started with Shabbat, holy time, not holy place. Erev Shabbat, getting ready as if a guest were coming. Candles, hands over the eyes. Kiddush over a cup. Two loaves of challah, covered. Melacha, the kinds of work set aside, and menuchah, real rest. The third meal at dusk, and Havdalah's braided candle and spices to carry the scent into the week. Then blessings through the day. Modeh Ani, thank you before you get up. Baruch, the word that opens almost every blessing. Hamotzi over bread, Birkat Hamazon after the meal, Shehecheyanu for firsts, and even a blessing inside grief. Then the year. The luach, a calendar kept by the moon. The shofar's cry, the sukkah's leafy roof, Hanukkah's lights, the seder's questions, counting the Omer to Shavuot. Tefillin on arm and head. Kosher, which means fit. And this last week: Talmud Torah, study as worship. Chavruta, learning in pairs. Kushya. Rashi on your shoulder. Hamaor shebah, the light inside it. La'asok. Look at the shape all that makes. The Torah itself begins it: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Six days of work, then a day that's different. Prayer at morning, afternoon and evening. A hundred small blessings, the Talmud says. Holidays that come back every year, so you meet yourself again. Nobody does all of it at once, and Jews keep these practices in very different ways. But a week can have a shape.

157.title: How the Torah is read
157.hook: a handwritten scroll, read aloud on Shabbat, Mondays and Thursdays
157.howItsDone: In synagogues the Torah scroll is taken from the ark and chanted aloud on Shabbat morning and afternoon and on Monday and Thursday mornings, as well as on festivals; the reader follows the text with a pointer called a yad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shavua: the camp of practices closed, and you chose three to keep. Your line was the week has a shape. Today a new camp opens: the text, one portion a week.

Most books are printed by a machine, thousands of copies at once. This one never is. Every letter is written by hand, with a quill, in ink, on parchment, by a trained scribe, one letter at a time. It's rolled on two wooden poles, dressed in a cloth cover, and kept in a cabinet at the front of the synagogue. When it comes out, people stand. Some reach out to touch it with the fringe of a prayer shawl, then kiss the fringe. And then someone reads it out loud, in a chant handed down from teacher to student.
screen: `EVERY LETTER BY HAND.` → `ROLLED ON TWO WOODEN POLES.` → `WHEN IT COMES OUT, PEOPLE STAND.`

segments.voice: Sefer Torah means a book of Torah: the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written by a sofer, a scribe, on sheets of parchment sewn together. The rules are exacting. Every letter must be formed correctly, and a single missing or broken letter can make the scroll unfit until it's fixed. There are no vowels in it and no punctuation, so the reader learns ahead of time how the words sound. The reader doesn't touch the parchment with a finger, but follows the line with a yad, a small pointer, often shaped like a hand. And it's chanted aloud in a set melody, with marks passed down for each word. When? On Shabbat morning, a full weekly portion. On Monday and Thursday mornings, and Shabbat afternoon, a shorter piece. Why Monday and Thursday? The Talmud connects it to the Israelites in the wilderness, who went three days without water and grew weak. The sages compared Torah to water, and arranged the readings so that three days never pass without it. Public reading appears in the Bible itself. In the book of Nehemiah, Ezra the scribe stands on a wooden platform and reads the Torah aloud to the whole people, men, women and all who could understand, and teachers explain it so everyone follows. That's the heart of it. In the synagogue, Torah isn't read silently in a corner. It's heard, together, out loud, with the whole room listening.

158.title: Fifty-four portions
158.hook: the Torah is divided into weekly portions and finished every year on Simchat Torah
158.howItsDone: Synagogues read the weekly portion on Shabbat morning in an annual cycle that ends and begins again on Simchat Torah; some Conservative and Reform congregations read a triennial cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sefer Torah: a handwritten scroll, chanted aloud on Shabbat, Mondays and Thursdays. Your line was heard, not just read.

Before streaming, a show came out one episode a week. Nobody could binge it. Everyone saw the same episode on the same night, and the next day at work, people talked about it. The Torah reading works a little like that, except the week never skips and the audience is spread across the world. On most Shabbat mornings, a synagogue in Buenos Aires, one in Paris and one in Melbourne are reading the same portion. People even name the week after it.
screen: `ONE EPISODE A WEEK.` → `THE SAME CHAPTER, WORLDWIDE.` → `THE WEEK HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: The word is parashah, a portion, a section set apart. The five books of Moses are divided into fifty-four portions, one read each Shabbat, starting in the fall. Fifty-four is more than the weeks some years have free, since festivals sometimes fall on Shabbat, so in some years two short portions are read together to keep the cycle on time. Each portion is named for its first important word or two. The first is Bereshit, in the beginning. The second is Noach, Noah. The third, Lech Lecha, go forth. So Jews will say, this is the week of Noach, the way you might say, it's the week of the big game. A bar or bat mitzvah is often remembered by its portion. And the cycle ends on a holiday you've met: Simchat Torah, rejoicing in the Torah. That day, the last lines of Deuteronomy are read, the death of Moses, and then, right away, the first lines of Genesis again. There's dancing with the scrolls. The story never stops; it just starts over. Here's a surprise: it wasn't always one year. The Talmud mentions that in the land of Israel, people finished the Torah in three years, in smaller pieces. In Babylonia, it was read in one, and the one-year cycle became the common practice. Some congregations today, especially in the Conservative and Reform movements, read a third of each portion instead, over a three-year cycle. Either way, the week has a portion, and the portion gives the week its name.

159.title: How to read a portion
159.hook: read it, find one question, see what Rashi asks, find one thing for your life
159.howItsDone: Many Jews prepare the weekly portion before Shabbat, some reading it twice in Hebrew and once in translation, and often with Rashi's commentary, then discuss it at the Shabbat table or in a class.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the parashah: fifty-four portions, each named for its first words, ending and beginning again on Simchat Torah. Your line was one portion a week.

You open the week's portion on a Sunday night with good intentions. It can be long: several chapters, sometimes over a hundred verses. By the third list of names, your eyes slide off the page. It's normal. People have felt this for centuries, which is why they built simple ways in. You don't have to take in the whole portion at once. You need a way of reading that fits a real week, with a job and dishes and sleep. Today, four steps that Jewish readers have used in one form or another for a very long time.
screen: `A HUNDRED VERSES ON A SUNDAY NIGHT.` → `YOUR EYES SLIDE OFF THE PAGE.` → `A WAY IN, FOR A REAL WEEK.`

segments.voice: Step one: read it. The Talmud gives a traditional minimum: read the week's portion twice in Hebrew and once in translation. For most people today that means the English, once, all the way through, without stopping to solve anything. Step two: find one question. Just one. Look for something odd: a word that repeats, a detail that seems unnecessary. Try it on the moment the people reach Mount Sinai. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "they encamped in the wilderness; and there Israel encamped before the mount." They camped, and then, in the same breath, Israel camped. Why say it twice? Step three: see what Rashi asks. Reading the Hebrew, Rashi caught something the English hides. The first verb is plural: they camped. The second is singular: he camped, as if the whole people were one person. Rashi explains: as one man, with one heart. And he adds a sharp little contrast. Every other stop on the journey came with complaining and quarreling. This one didn't. Before anything could be given at that mountain, the people had to arrive as one. Step four: find one thing for your life. Maybe it's this: a family dinner, a team, a group chat the night before a big day. When did you last arrive somewhere as one, and not as a list of separate complaints? An early teacher in the Mishnah named Ben Bag Bag said of the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. You don't have to turn the whole portion every week. One verse, turned well, can last seven days.
screen: `READ IT ONCE, ALL THE WAY.` · `FIND ONE QUESTION.` · `SEE WHAT RASHI ASKS.` · `FIND ONE THING FOR YOUR LIFE.` · then, large: `ONE VERSE A WEEK.`

160.title: Called up to the Torah
160.hook: people are called up to say a blessing before and after each section
160.howItsDone: During the Torah reading, members of the congregation are called by their Hebrew names to recite blessings before and after each section while the reader chants; seven are called on Shabbat morning and three on Mondays and Thursdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi's question at Sinai: read it, find one question, see what Rashi asks, find one thing for your life. Your line was one verse a week.

It's Shabbat morning. The scroll is open on the reading table, and the room goes quiet. Someone at the table calls out a Hebrew name, the person's own and their parents'. A person in the congregation stands up, a little nervous, and walks to the front. Maybe it's their first time since their bar or bat mitzvah. Maybe their grandmother is watching. Maybe they've just had a baby, or are about to get married, or it's the anniversary of a parent's death. They step up to the scroll. They don't have to read a word of it. They just have to bless.
screen: `A HEBREW NAME IS CALLED.` → `SOMEONE WALKS TO THE FRONT.` → `THEY DON'T READ. THEY BLESS.`

segments.voice: The word is aliyah, going up. The reading table often stands on a raised platform, the bimah, so you literally go up to it. But the word means more than stairs: being called to the Torah is an honor, a going up in spirit. On Shabbat morning the portion is divided into seven sections, and seven people are called, one for each, with an extra one at the end. On Mondays and Thursdays, three. Traditionally the first goes to a kohen, a descendant of the priests, the second to a levi, and the rest to anyone. Here's what happens. The person looks at the place in the scroll and says the blessing before. It begins Barchu, bless the Lord who is blessed, and it thanks God for choosing Israel and giving the Torah. The reader chants the section while the person stands beside them, following along. Then the blessing after: thanking God, who gave us a Torah of truth and planted eternal life in our midst. And they step aside for the next. In Orthodox synagogues, men are called up. In Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative synagogues, women are called up too. The same word has another life: when a Jew moves to the land of Israel, that's also called making aliyah, going up. So this week's four days fit together: a handwritten scroll, heard aloud. Fifty-four portions. A way to read one. And now, a way to stand beside it, and go up.
screen: `ALIYAH: GOING UP.` · `SEVEN ON SHABBAT, THREE ON WEEKDAYS.` · `A BLESSING BEFORE AND AFTER.` · `A TORAH OF TRUTH, ETERNAL LIFE.` · then, large: `GO UP.`

161.title: Bereshit: why begin with bet?
161.hook: the Torah opens with its second letter, closed on three sides and open ahead (Genesis Rabbah 1:10)
161.howItsDone: Parashat Bereshit, Genesis 1:1–6:8, is read on the Shabbat after Simchat Torah, and students traditionally begin their study of it with Rashi's comments on the first verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aliyah: going up to the scroll to bless before and after. Your line was go up.

Every alphabet starts somewhere. English starts with A. Hebrew starts with aleph. So you'd expect the Torah to start with aleph. It doesn't. Its very first word is Bereshit, in the beginning, and it starts with the second letter, bet. The rabbis noticed, and asked: why would the Torah skip its own first letter? It seems like a tiny thing. But in the study hall, a tiny thing is a door.
screen: `A, ALEPH, THE FIRST LETTER.` → `THE TORAH STARTS WITH BET.` → `A TINY THING IS A DOOR.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in English: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In Hebrew, the first word is Bereshit, and its first letter is bet. Look at its shape. It's like a square bracket: a line along the top, a line down the right side, a line along the bottom, and open on the left. Hebrew reads right to left, so that open side faces forward, into the rest of the text. The midrash, Genesis Rabbah, asks: why was the world created with a bet? Because just as the bet is closed on three sides and open on one, you are not meant to ask what is above, what is below, what came before. Only from the day the world was created, and onward. It's a surprising answer. It sets a limit: some questions, about what came before the beginning, are closed. But it opens a road: everything after is yours to explore. The same passage gives another reason. Bet begins bracha, blessing; aleph begins a word for curse. So the Torah starts with the letter of blessing. And Rashi, whom you met last week, adds a grammar puzzle. The first words, he says, don't quite mean in the beginning. They mean something closer to, in the beginning of God's creating. Read that way, the verse isn't listing what was made first; it's the start of a longer sentence. So the Torah opens mid-sentence, with a letter that looks forward. The midrash puts the lesson in its shape: a wall behind, and the way open ahead.
screen: `THE FIRST LETTER IS BET.` · `CLOSED ON THREE SIDES, OPEN AHEAD.` · `BET FOR BLESSING.` · `IN THE BEGINNING OF CREATING.` · then, large: `OPEN AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Picture the letter bet: a roof, a wall behind you, a floor, and an open side in front. Let the wall be everything already done, yesterday's mistakes, old worries, what you can't change, holding you up instead of pulling you back. Then look toward the open side, and find one step ahead of you today, just one.
Bereshit. In the beginning: the first word of the Torah and the name of its first portion, starting with a bet, open ahead.
Your line: open ahead. Tomorrow, the story of creation gets told a second time. Day one hundred sixty-one, done.
